title: Questions that must be answered before a reasonable decision
description: The information ledger the brief asked for: what we know, what we do not know, and precisely what has to be true before a decision is defensible. Blocking means a decision downstream of this question is unsafe to make. Where 'what we know' cites a source, the source is the league's or a regulator's own page, not a summary of it.

rows.question: Is this a paper (model-only) programme, or are real wagers intended?
rows.why: Everything else — staking, legal review, prize structure, record retention, responsible-gambling copy — changes character the moment money moves. An agent must not assume the answer.
rows.known: The brief asks for origination, gates and a rewarded leaderboard, which implies real stake allocation, but the repo contains no bankroll policy, no operator agreement and no jurisdiction.
rows.lack: Explicit intent, bankroll size and the risk mandate.
rows.obtain: Owner decision; record it in COORDINATION.md as a one-line mandate.
rows.default: Treat as paper until stated otherwise, and generate no bet slips with monetary stakes.
rows.no_source_reason: Owner-decision question: no external source can answer what only the owner can decide. Every external fact this question depends on is cited separately.

rows.question: What is the source of truth for opening and closing NFL lines, and do we have a licence to store it?
rows.why: Without line history there is no backtest, no closing-line value metric, no way to measure correlation against market prices, and no proof our number beats theirs. It is the largest single gap in the programme.
rows.known: The NFL's real-time official play-by-play, Next Gen Stats and official betting data feed are distributed exclusively by Genius Sports under a deal extended through the end of the 2029 season; the three official operator partners receive access through that arrangement.
rows.lack: Any point-in-time historical line dataset (openers, mid-week ticks, closers) plus the storage and derived-works rights that come with it.
rows.obtain: Purchase a licensed historical lines feed or negotiate operator data-sharing; check the licence permits retention and derived publication.
rows.default: No validated claim of market-beating ability; the leaderboard stays in research mode with paper stakes.

rows.question: What is the authoritative settlement source for player props, and where do operators differ from it?
rows.why: A prop edge is worthless if the operator settles on a different stat definition than the one we model; a genuine statistical edge disappears into official-scoring-judgment variance.
rows.known: House rules filed with regulators define settlement sources and void or reprice behaviour per market family, and they are version-stamped documents.
rows.lack: A per-market matrix of our stat source versus each operator's settlement source, maintained against the current rule version.
rows.obtain: Build the matrix from each operator's filed house rules, reconciled against official league statistics, and diff it on every rule-version bump.
rows.default: Trade only spreads and totals, where settlement is unambiguous.

rows.question: Which jurisdictions do we operate in, and at what age and product availability?
rows.why: Legality, tax treatment, promo availability and even which markets exist differ by state; a strategy that assumes a market the state bans cannot be executed at all.
rows.known: Regulated state markets exist and each publishes its own revenue and reporting returns, which we already cite for hold calibration.
rows.lack: Our operator/account jurisdictions, geolocation settings and each state's market restrictions.
rows.obtain: Owner states jurisdiction; then pull that state regulator's rules page directly.
rows.default: Assume research-only: no placement, no automation of wagering.

rows.question: What are the risk limits: unit size, weekly exposure, per-game and per-cluster caps, and the drawdown that triggers a stop?
rows.why: Staking rules are the difference between a positive-expectation model and a ruined bankroll. Kelly is a growth optimum, not a safety rule, and full Kelly is unusable on estimated probabilities.
rows.known: The standard remedy is fractional Kelly with parameter uncertainty folded in; a leaderboard that scores raw return rewards the same ruin risk it is supposed to filter.
rows.lack: The owner's loss tolerance and the correlated-exposure constraints that make a per-bet cap insufficient.
rows.obtain: Owner sets three numbers: unit, weekly cap, kill-switch drawdown. Everything else is derivable from those.
rows.default: Quarter-Kelly on our own probability estimate, 1 unit per single, 2 units per game cluster, 0.5 units per prop combo, no live betting.

rows.question: Which designation-to-availability mapping do we use, and how is it estimated rather than inherited from folklore?
rows.why: The injury model's entire magnitude flows from P(play | designation, practice history). A hard-coded 50% for Questionable is the most common and least defended assumption in this space.
rows.known: The league's official definitions are qualitative: Questionable means it is uncertain whether the player will play, Doubtful means it is unlikely, Out means he will not play. Probable was eliminated precisely because roughly 95% of players so labelled played, and a player certain to play is not listed in the Game Status Report at all.
rows.lack: Our own empirical table of P(play) by designation, practice trajectory, position and game day, plus P(active but limited snaps), which no designation describes.
rows.obtain: Ingest the league's report archive (the public page exposes season and week selectors back to 1965), join to final inactive lists and snap data we own, then fit per-position hazard tables.
rows.default: Use designation as a categorical feature only; converting a tag to a probability in production is a code-review reject until a fitted table exists.

rows.question: Where and when does the final inactive list officially appear, and can we capture it programmatically?
rows.why: The swing between Friday's report and the Sunday inactive list is the largest single information event of the week; if we cannot capture it at the right time, our model is systematically stale at release.
rows.known: Game-status designations are filed on the practice-report cadence, and club-side documents mark status changes explicitly.
rows.lack: A verified official endpoint and deadline for inactive lists. Secondary sources say about 90 minutes before kickoff; no official confirmation was found in this pass.
rows.obtain: Verify against the league's gameday operations documentation and club pages, then instrument a Sunday capture job with a timestamp log and record the finding.
rows.default: Friday 4pm ET is the last committed number; hold no position into Sunday until inactives are verified from an official source.

rows.question: Do we have the depth-chart and next-man-up inputs, given no official league depth-chart endpoint could be found?
rows.why: The brief's core requirement — knowing when a second, third or fourth-stringer replaces a starter — is a depth-chart problem, not an injury-report problem. The report says who is out; only the chart says who is in.
rows.known: Roster architecture is officially documented: 53-man active/inactive, 54 or 55 via practice-squad elevation, a 47 or 48 gameday roster, IR four-game minimum with up to eight designations to return, PUP and NFI clearing after four games. That lets us derive the set of eligible replacements.
rows.lack: A verified official NFL.com depth-chart endpoint: the expected path returned the league's 404 page and the transactions path redirected. Depth charts appear to live on club-operated pages, in 32 different layouts.
rows.obtain: Either build 32 club-page parsers, or derive a shadow depth chart from our own snap-share logs joined to the official availability file — we recommend the second because it is source-stable.
rows.default: Use the derived shadow chart and label every deficiency number 'estimated, not official'.

rows.question: What data are we permitted to collect, and under what terms?
rows.why: An architecture built on scraping an exclusively distributed feed is not a footnote, it is a rebuild risk: it can invalidate the pipeline, the site's public claims and the prize competition at once.
rows.known: One distributor holds exclusive rights to official real-time play-by-play, NGS and the official betting feed for media and operators; the league's own terms govern use of its public pages; several state regulators publish operator house rules and market data openly.
rows.lack: A reviewed position on our collection methods (league terms, robots policy, licensed feeds, operator APIs) and the redistribution rights for anything the site publishes.
rows.obtain: Legal review of the collection plan against the league's terms and the distributor's licence, then encode the resulting allowlist in the collector config and enforce it in CI.
rows.default: Read only the sources registered in data/sources.json; quote with links; buy nothing without approval.

rows.question: What hold and vig do we assume per market family, and is that number measured or folklore?
rows.why: The hold assumption sets the break-even hurdle, which sets the edge threshold, which sets how many bets we should ever take. It compounds violently inside parlays.
rows.known: Regulators publish the raw material: Illinois exposes monthly sports wagering reports with CSV and a Sport Detail Report; New York publishes statewide and per-operator weekly and monthly Excel files; Nevada's control standards require books to report wagers accepted, amounts paid, taxable win and win-to-write percentage per sport and for parlay cards separately.
rows.lack: The actual figures, opened and parsed. Two plausible Nevada landing paths returned 404, so we publish no Nevada number, and the widely repeated 'parlay hold in the 30s' remains unverified by us.
rows.obtain: A one-time scripted download of the Illinois and New York report sets into data/market_hold.csv, refreshed monthly with the regulator's own publication lag.
rows.default: Model singles at -110 using the 4.55% theoretical hold on turnover (a 4.76% overround), and treat any parlay as strictly worse by an unmeasured additive, so parlays must clear a higher hurdle.

rows.question: How do we price a Same Game Parlay: our own joint distribution, or the operator's combined price?
rows.why: Correlation is exactly why naive multiplication of single-leg prices overstates parlay value. Whose price we benchmark against determines whether our apparent edge is real or an artefact of ignoring the operator's correlation model.
rows.known: House rules permit correlated legs only inside a Same Game Parlay and reprice the SGP when a leg is void or pushed; a parlay outside the SGP may never contain related outcomes. Nevada requires parlay-card win percentages to be reported separately from straight sports wagering.
rows.lack: A comparison of our joint-priced SGP fair value against posted SGP prices across a sample, to see how much of our edge the operator has already taken.
rows.obtain: Snapshot SGP prices with their component singles for a full season, then measure the implied correlation and the residual edge.
rows.default: Claim no parlay edge; treat singles as the only market that can be validated by design in v1.

rows.question: What counts as a skill strategy on the leaderboard, and what kills an entrant's claim?
rows.why: A rewarded leaderboard without a skill definition rewards the luckiest entrant and turns the programme into a variance lottery — the failure the brief names directly.
rows.known: The forecasting literature provides the tooling: White's Reality Check, Hansen's Superior Predictive Ability test, Romano and Wolf's stepwise extension, deflated Sharpe ratios and paired stationary bootstraps all exist to answer whether the best of many candidates truly beats a benchmark once how-many-you-tried is accounted for.
rows.lack: Our thresholds: minimum bet count, minimum seasons, adopted multiple-testing correction, concentration cap and promotion rule.
rows.obtain: Adopt data/validation_gates.json as the competition constitution and freeze it before entries open.
rows.default: Rank on the 95% lower confidence bound of expected value; no promotion without passing G-1 to G-13; prizes deferred until gates pass.

rows.question: What prize or reward structure is lawful for a strategy competition with money at stake?
rows.why: Entry fee plus chance plus prize is the lottery shape. A competition whose ranking is partly luck and whose entry is paid sits on the wrong side of several lines, including the league's own posture on contests.
rows.known: The league requires betting partners to observe strict integrity rules, prohibits its personnel from betting and from daily fantasy, and treats prediction markets as sports betting — a fair indicator of how tightly the surrounding product space is policed.
rows.lack: Counsel's view on free-to-enter skill-based contest rules, eligibility, disclosure, tax reporting and payout rails.
rows.obtain: Legal opinion, published official rules, free entry, skill-based ranking, prizes kept away from the operator accounts we bet through.
rows.default: Rewards are non-cash: compute credits, staking allocation and internal capital promotion.

rows.question: How much sample do our bankroll and calendar actually allow, given the required n is enormous?
rows.why: This arithmetic decides whether the programme is plausible. An edge too small to detect within a decade of NFL Sundays is not an edge we can act on, whatever the backtest says.
rows.known: Break-even at -110 is 52.38%. Distinguishing a 55.0% strategy from that hurdle with 80% power at a one-sided 5% test requires 2,243 bets; a 57% strategy needs 719 (computed by engine/stats.required_sample, published on the Validation page). Inverting it: a strategy that takes 150 bets a season can only prove a true hit rate of about 62.4%.
rows.lack: Our realistic bet volume per season under a defensible edge threshold, and therefore our minimum detectable edge.
rows.obtain: Simulate the trade-off curve, pick the edge threshold that yields an acceptable sample per season, or accept multi-season validation.
rows.default: Two promotions per season maximum, pre-registered expected bet volume per entrant, and the detectable-edge curve published on the site.

rows.question: Which non-market inputs do we trust at v1: schedule, availability, rest, venue, or none?
rows.why: This sets the size of the first release, not its validity: a totals model can start from priors plus availability and add features later.
rows.known: The official schedule and operations calendar give rest days, short weeks and venues; availability comes from the injury report.
rows.lack: A verified weather source (NOAA/NWS not checked in this pass), a dome/outdoor classification list, and travel or timezone effects we are willing to code with citations.
rows.obtain: A short verification pass on the federal weather endpoint and the schedule fields; write each into the feature register with its source and update cadence.
rows.default: Ship v1 with schedule plus availability only, and state that limitation on the model card.

rows.question: Do we use referee-crew information at all, given officiating-linked markets are prohibited?
rows.why: A tempting feature that pulls the model toward markets the league refuses to offer and toward data we cannot source officially. It needs a policy decision, not a data source.
rows.known: The league prohibits Officiating-Related markets as a class, including assignments, penalties and replays.
rows.lack: Whether crew tendencies may inform a legal market (spread or total) even though no officiating market may be offered.
rows.obtain: Adopt the conservative internal line — no crew feature, documented in the model card — and revisit only with legal input.
rows.default: Excluded by design.

rows.question: How stale is our information at release, and what lag between an official update and our re-price is acceptable?
rows.why: Sets the ingestion architecture (event-triggered polling versus streaming) and whether we can credibly claim a Friday-close advantage.
rows.known: The official report is published on a practice-day cadence and club documents mark status changes, so minute-level polling is unnecessary but event-triggered polling is essential.
rows.lack: Measured publish-to-price latency once the collector runs in production.
rows.obtain: Instrument the collector with a publish-to-price stopwatch and publish the p95 on the site.
rows.default: Re-price on each official report drop and on any transaction event, with a hard stop 30 minutes before our bet cut-off.

rows.question: Which sibling branches do we merge, and who arbitrates overlapping claims?
rows.why: A coordination decision, not a modelling one — but it decides whether the published site is one coherent system or four competing ones.
rows.known: Four sessions each branched from the same commit and each wrote a COORDINATION.md claiming all tasks; one already published a full static site under docs/, two published only claims.
rows.lack: A designated integration owner with authority to merge and publish.
rows.obtain: This session nominated itself as integrator on the open-remote evidence, preserved every sibling's files, and logged the handoff. If another session objects, the fix is a rebase and re-verification, not a deletion.
rows.default: Merge all non-conflicting files from all four branches, resolve COORDINATION.md by union, publish the union.

rows.question: Where does the automation run, and who owns the credentials and the schedule?
rows.why: 'No manual input' is an infrastructure claim. Without a host, ingestion, gate evaluation and rebuilds silently stop, and a stale dashboard is worse than none.
rows.known: Everything in this repo runs on the Python standard library plus a static build, so one small VM or a scheduled GitHub Action is enough for a weekly cadence.
rows.lack: A target environment, service account, alerting channel and a retention policy for raw snapshots, which audit requires.
rows.obtain: Owner provisions a runner and storage for raw captures; then wire a nightly job with a dead-man switch.
rows.default: Site rebuilds on push only; the as-of date is printed on every page so staleness is visible.
rows.no_source_reason: Owner-decision question: no external source can answer what only the owner can decide. Every external fact this question depends on is cited separately.

rows.question: What is our stance on prediction markets as an execution venue or benchmark?
rows.why: They price the same events with different rules and different hold, inside a live regulatory argument; using one changes both the edge estimate and the compliance surface.
rows.known: The league treats prediction markets on sports outcomes as sports betting under its policy, prohibits personnel participation, restricts their advertising in broadcasts, has written to them about prohibited wagers, and omitted them from its 2026 operator partnerships.
rows.lack: Whether we may execute there, and whether their quotes are usable as a closing benchmark for CLV.
rows.obtain: Owner decision plus counsel; if used for execution, exclude their prices from the CLV benchmark or document why not.
rows.default: Not an execution venue, not part of the closing-line benchmark.

rows.question: What is our tradable market universe after the league's prohibited classes are subtracted?
rows.why: The injury-derived feature set is legitimate as an input, but a bet whose subject is an injury, or a one-person one-play outcome, is one the league asks operators not to offer. The universe must be fixed before any strategy is scored.
rows.known: The league's published prohibited classes: Inherently Objectionable (including player injuries, fan safety, misconduct), Officiating-Related (assignments, penalties, replays), Determinable by One Person in One Play (kicker to miss, QB's first pass incomplete), and Pre-Determined outcomes (will the QB start this week).
rows.lack: Our exclusion list as a matcher over market names, and a test that it cannot be bypassed by a renamed market.
rows.obtain: engine/compliance.py already encodes the four classes; extend with per-operator market-name tests and re-run every ingestion cycle.
rows.default: Game spread, game total, team totals and player stat markets that are not injury, officiating or single-play proxies; refuse everything else.

rows.question: What happens when the numbers stop beating the close: what is the demotion rule?
rows.why: Pre-committing a kill rule is the cheapest defence against the sunk-cost drift that keeps losing strategies funded.
rows.known: A live CLV monitor with a trip threshold and a demotion ladder, using the same multiple-comparison machinery that promotes.
rows.lack: The threshold, who flips the switch, and the review cadence.
rows.obtain: Adopt G-11's decay test as the demotion rule and report it in the executive summary every week.
rows.default: Auto-demote to research mode when the rolling CLV lower bound stays below zero for 250 bets.

rows.question: How do we prove no non-public information entered the model?
rows.why: Using leaked lineup or injury information would be precisely the conduct the league, its partners and regulators are built to detect, and it would destroy the programme and possibly more.
rows.known: The league requires personnel to sign an annual gambling policy prohibiting the sharing of inside information, monitors betting patterns through its partners, assigns an integrity representative to every club, and states that unusual patterns may indicate a leak of non-public information.
rows.lack: A written data-provenance attestation per input and an access policy that makes non-public channels unreachable by construction.
rows.obtain: The source register is the input allowlist; make CI fail on any input not listed in it.
rows.default: Only sources in data/sources.json may be read, enforced in the collector config rather than by convention.

rows.question: What must the site show about itself to stay honest?
rows.why: A dashboard that hides its unverified cells will be trusted like a live model, which is how an empty field turns into a decision.
rows.known: The brief requires unconfirmable values to be left blank and flagged; we enforce that at build time, and every source carries a verification level so a reader can see that INDEX-MEANS is not FETCHED.
rows.lack: Whether the owner wants the as-of timestamps, the review page and the 'no Nevada number published' stance presented that prominently.
rows.obtain: Owner reviews the Flagged for Review page after deployment and adjusts prominence, not substance.
rows.default: Keep the current prominence: blanks, flags and verification levels stay on the surface of every table.
